newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro quotes Bible but firmly at odds with Pope.
newsitem.headline: Castro quotes Bible but firmly at odds with Pope.

text.p: Cuban President Fidel Castro quoted the Bible on Sunday, two days before an historic audience with Pope John Paul, but set himself squarely at odds with the Pontiff on the Vatican's taboo subject of birth control.

The veteran communist, star of a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit, told a closing news conference he was not going to deliver a lesson on Marx and Engels. But he said since there was no hope of life on Mars, the earth's population must be limited.
"We are not living in an earthly paradise," Castro said.
"As the Bible says, there were Adam and Eve and that was that. Now there are a billion of us. This is a new phenomenon," the 70-year-old revolutionary said to gales of laughter.

The world's population was exploding at a "terrible rhythm", Castro said. "This requires planning, birth control. I think a lot of people are convinced of this. I think the Catholic Church itself, in fact, is convinced of this."
The Vatican's Secretary of State, Angelo Sodano, renewed the Pope's cast-iron opposition to artificial means of limiting the population in his address to the five-day summit.
Castro is scheduled to have an historic audience with the Pope on Tuesday at the Vatican.

The long awaited meeting between the communist icon and one of the world's leading anti-communist crusaders is expected to cement sometimes prickly relations between the Caribbean island and the Roman Catholic Church.

"In the days of Marx and Engels even, there were no references to these (population) restrictions. Communism could be achieved by an increase in production methods," said Castro, who has ruled Cuba for nearly 38 years.
"I'm not going to give you a lesson in Marxism here...but at that time it seemed there were no limits to human resources, natural resources. However, they are limited.

"Unfortunately, on the moon, on Mars, Venus, Jupiter, nowhere in the heavens as far as we know, is it possible for mankind to live. So we can't hold out hope of a new Christopher Columbus to discover lands elsewhere outside the planet.

"We have to administer ourselves...I think that in this world that is so complex and so selfish that we have to be flexible on the question of birth control and in the procedure to achieve it," Castro said.
"Respect must be shown for all beliefs and faiths."
However Castro, who was educated by Jesuit priests as a child, did agree with the Pope on one thing.
"Abortion is legal in my country but we don't like it. It is not advisable. It's not that convenient, praiseworthy," he said.
"We don't like divorces either. It's not convenient but it's allowed by law," he said, adding that unhappy marriages were an "excessive sacrifice" to expect of people.
The Vatican calls abortion murder and frowns on divorce.
Castro, who has been surrounded by tight security in Rome, clearly lapped up the limelight at the packed news conference where most questions were directed at him.
Chatting amiably to reporters as the event ended, he said he planned to take a "message of peace" to the Pope, but added: "I'm not going to get into theological issues at all."
